topic: the 1917 French Army mutinies -- soldiers refused to attack but almost none deserted, and far fewer were executed than sentenced
title: France's WWI Army Mutinied in 1917, But Fewer Than 50 Were Executed
description: AI-narrated commentary on the 1917 French Army mutinies -- when nearly half of France's WWI infantry divisions refused to keep attacking, but the way it actually played out (and ended) is stranger than the popular idea of a 'mutiny.'

hook_candidates.text: A 1917 mutiny where a French army refused to fight, but not one soldier deserted.
What happens when half an army refuses to fight, but nobody deserts?
A mutiny doesn't always mean soldiers turn against their own side. In 1917, French troops proved that.
In the spring of 1917, tens of thousands of French soldiers made an unspoken deal with their own generals.

share_trigger: A viewer sends this to their grandfather who insists mutinies always end in mass executions, because they want to prove him wrong.
contradicted_belief: Most people think a mutiny means soldiers desert or refuse to fight, but not this time.
closing_comment: 554 men were sentenced to death, but fewer than 50 were actually shot, and that gap says everything about this mutiny.

sources.note: Petain's courts martial sentenced 554 mutineers to death; only a small fraction were ever actually executed.
Details the disputed execution count (est. 26-50) against 3,400 courts martial and 554 death sentences.
